title: Urinary Catheterization: Principles, Female and Male Procedures, and Safety
introduction: Urinary catheterization is a strictly sterile invasive procedure providing direct bladder access for diagnostic sampling, output monitoring, surgical protection, or relief of urinary retention. Thorough knowledge of sex-specific urethral anatomy, catheter types and French sizing, contraindications, aseptic insertion steps, and complication prevention minimizes trauma and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI).
learningOutcomes: 5.1 Define urinary catheterization, compare female and male urethral anatomy, and state diagnostic, therapeutic, and surgical indications alongside contraindications.
5.2 Identify catheter anatomical parts, classify catheter types (intermittent, indwelling/Foley, suprapubic, external condom, coude, 3-way), and select appropriate French sizes across age and sex.
5.3 Perform comprehensive pre-catheterization assessment, formulate nursing diagnoses/objectives, and prepare sterile catheterization equipment.
5.4 Execute step-by-step sterile female and male urethral catheterization procedures, troubleshooting measures, and post-insertion securing/drainage care.
5.5 Recognize and prevent major complications of catheterization (UTI, paraphimosis, stricture, perforation, obstruction, bladder spasms).

content.heading: Definition, Urethral Anatomy, Indications, Contraindications, and Pre-Procedure Assessment
content.body: Urinary catheterization is the strictly sterile introduction of a thin flexible catheter into the urinary bladder—most commonly retrograde via the urethra or surgically through the lower abdomen (suprapubic)—performed only when clinically necessary. Anatomically, the female urethra is ~3.7–6.2 cm long, opening as an anteroposterior slit anterior to the vaginal orifice and ~2.5 cm posterior to the glans clitoris (it may recede superiorly into the vagina in older women). The male urethra is 18–20 cm long, extending from the internal orifice at the bladder neck through prostatic, membranous, and spongy segments to the glans tip. Indications span three domains: (1) Diagnostic—uncontaminated culture specimen, accurate urine output monitoring, post-void residual volume, urinary tract imaging; (2) Therapeutic—acute urinary retention (e.g., BPH, blood clots), chronic obstruction with hydronephrosis, continuous bladder irrigation, neurogenic bladder decompression, intravesical medication/chemotherapy instillation, and selected urinary incontinence/bedridden care; and (3) Surgical—keeping the bladder empty before/during/after abdominopelvic, urological, or gynaecological surgery to improve visualization, prevent accidental bladder injury, and protect perineal sutures. Contraindications include suspected urethral trauma (blood at the meatus—insertion worsens injury!), gross haematuria, urethral infection, urethral pain, low bladder compliance, and patient refusal. Pre-procedure assessment checks last voiding time/fluid intake, urge to void, dysuria/frequency/hesitancy, incontinence, suprapubic palpation (firm rounded mass) and percussion (dullness indicating full bladder), antiseptic allergies, prior catheterization, positioning ability, and signs of anxiety (shaky hands, facial tension), guiding diagnoses of Altered Urinary Elimination, Urinary Retention, Anxiety, Risk for Impaired Skin Integrity, and Pain.

content.heading: Catheter Parts, Types, French Sizing, and Short-Term vs. Long-Term Methods
content.body: An indwelling Foley catheter features six parts: catheter tip, drainage eye, balloon seal, catheter shaft, drainage funnel, and inflation funnel/balloon port (marked with recommended sterile water volume). Four primary catheter types exist: (1) Intermittent (Straight) Catheter—inserted temporarily for 5–10 minutes to empty the bladder and removed immediately; (2) Indwelling (Foley) Catheter—retained for days or weeks via a water-filled internal balloon (including 2-way and 3-way irrigation catheters, plus curved-tip Coude catheters); (3) Suprapubic Catheter—inserted surgically through a small suprapubic incision for continuous drainage (key alternative when urethral trauma exists); and (4) External Condom Catheter—adheres externally to the penis or pubic area for incontinence management. Catheter lumen diameter is measured on the French scale (Fr)—smaller numbers mean narrower tubes; always use the smallest effective size to reduce trauma, noting standard clinical sizing: Children (8–10 Fr), Adult Females (14–16 Fr, commonly 16 Fr), and Adult Males (20–22 Fr—stiffer to negotiate the longer male urethra). Short-term catheterization serves temporary obstruction, pelvic/bowel surgery, childbirth bladder drainage, or post-injury clot removal, whereas Long-term catheterization serves critically ill patients, refractory incontinence, or neuropathic bladder (with suprapubic or condom catheters as alternatives).

content.heading: Step-by-Step Female and Male Urethral Catheterization Techniques
content.body: Assemble a sterile catheterization pack (under-drape, fenestrated perineal drape, sterile gloves, antiseptic lotion, water-soluble lubricant, cotton balls/gauze, catheter, forceps, basin), prefilled 10–30 mL syringe, specimen container, angle-poise lamp, closed drainage bag (uribag), Velcro leg strap/tape, disposal bag, waterproof pad, and extra sheet. For Female Catheterization: explain/gain consent, ensure privacy/lighting, wash perineum with warm water/soap first, position in dorsal recumbent (knees flexed, thighs relaxed) or Sims's position, wash hands and don sterile gloves, drape sterile field, test indwelling balloon integrity and deflate leaving syringe attached, lubricate tip 1–2 inches, separate labia with non-dominant hand (now contaminated—maintain separation continuously), cleanse with forceps and fresh antiseptic cotton balls anterior-to-posterior (clitoris to anus, outer to inner folds, meatus last), instruct client to take a slow deep breath to relax perineal muscles, gently insert 5–7.5 cm until urine flows (never force) plus 1 extra inch for indwelling catheters, drain NO MORE THAN 750 mL at once to prevent hypotension, inflate balloon with sterile water per manufacturer volume, tug gently for resistance then advance slightly off the bladder neck, connect closed uribag kept below bladder level without kinks, and tape to upper thigh with slack. For Male Catheterization: position supine with thighs slightly apart, generously lubricate catheter 15–18 cm (and instil local anaesthetic lubricant gel proximally while occluding distal urethra; cooling gel to 4°C reduces transient stinging), grasp penis with non-dominant hand, retract foreskin in uncircumcised males, cleanse circularly from meatus toward shaft base, hold penis at a 90° angle pulling gently upward to straighten the urethra, advance catheter 15–20 cm (to the Y-hub) until urine flows plus 1 inch (if resistance occurs, ask client to breathe deeply/bear down or adjust angle; NEVER force—stop and notify charge nurse for possible stricture/BPH), inflate balloon only after urine return, ALWAYS reduce retracted foreskin immediately afterward, and secure catheter to upper thigh or lower abdomen with penis directed toward the chest and slack for nocturnal erection.

content.heading: Troubleshooting, Home Care, Documentation, and Complications
content.body: If urine does not flow immediately after insertion, ask the client to take a deep breath (relaxes perineal/abdominal muscles), rotate the catheter slightly (frees drainage eye from bladder wall), or raise the head of the bed to boost bladder pressure. For clients with indwelling catheters, showers are recommended over tub baths to reduce ascending bacterial entry; for home intermittent self-catheterization, clean technique suffices (wash thoroughly, boil catheter 20 minutes, dry, and store cleanly). Document insertion time, catheter size, sterile water volume in balloon, presence/absence of bleeding or inflammation, patient tolerance, and urine amount, colour, and odour. Major complications include: Urinary Tract Infection (urethritis, cystitis, pyelonephritis, transient bacteraemia—the MOST COMMON long-term complication), Paraphimosis (from failing to reduce the foreskin post-procedure), urethral strictures, urethral perforation/injury, bleeding, pain from bag traction, catheter obstruction from sediment (relieved by flushing), altered micturition, and painful bladder spasms causing extrinsic urine leakage (managed with anticholinergics such as oxybutynin).

inTextQuestions.question: Why must no more than 750 mL of urine be drained at one time during urinary catheterization?
What clinical sign at the urethral meatus is an absolute warning sign/contraindication against urethral catheter insertion, and what alternative route can be used?
inTextQuestions.answer: Blood at the meatus (indicating urethral trauma, which catheter insertion can worsen). Suprapubic catheterization (or external condom catheter for incontinence) is the alternative.

inTextQuestions.question: What causes paraphimosis after male catheterization, and why must slack be left when taping a male patient's catheter toward the chest?
inTextQuestions.answer: Paraphimosis is caused by failing to reduce the retracted foreskin back over the glans after catheterization. Leaving slack prevents tension and accommodates natural nocturnal penile erection, while directing the penis toward the chest prevents penoscrotal angle irritation.

inTextQuestions.question: State the standard French catheter sizes for children, adult females, and adult males.
inTextQuestions.answer: Children: 8 Fr and 10 Fr; Adult females: 14 Fr and 16 Fr; Adult males: 20 Fr and 22 Fr.

saqs.question: Explain why a patient undergoing non-urological abdominopelvic surgery may require urinary catheterization, and list five contraindications to urethral catheterization.
saqs.answer: Surgical catheterization keeps the bladder empty to give the surgeon a clearer view and safer palpation of internal tissues, prevents accidental bladder injury, and prevents urine from contaminating perineal sutures. Five contraindications: blood at the meatus (urethral trauma), gross haematuria, urethral infection, urethral pain/discomfort, and patient refusal (also low bladder compliance).

saqs.question: List the six parts of an indwelling Foley catheter and differentiate intermittent, indwelling, suprapubic, and external condom catheters.
saqs.answer: Parts: catheter tip, drainage eye, balloon seal, catheter shaft, drainage funnel, and inflation funnel/balloon port. Types: Intermittent (temporary 5–10 min drainage), Indwelling/Foley (held in place days/weeks by water-filled balloon), Suprapubic (surgically placed through lower abdomen for continuous drainage), External condom (non-invasive sheath adhering externally for incontinence).

saqs.question: Compare the anatomical length, cleansing technique, insertion depth, and securing method between female and male urethral catheterization.
saqs.answer: Female: urethra 3.7–6.2 cm; cleanse labia/meatus anterior-to-posterior (meatus last) with fresh swabs; insert 5–7.5 cm (+1 inch for balloon); secure to upper thigh with slack. Male: urethra 18–20 cm; retract foreskin, cleanse circularly from meatus to base; hold penis at 90° upward, lubricate 15–18 cm, insert 15–20 cm (to Y-hub) +1 inch; reduce foreskin; secure to thigh or lower abdomen directed toward chest with slack.

saqs.question: Outline three troubleshooting actions if urine fails to flow immediately after catheter insertion, and explain why a shower is safer than a tub bath with an indwelling catheter.
saqs.answer: Troubleshooting: (1) ask the client to take a deep breath to relax perineal/abdominal muscles, (2) rotate the catheter slightly in case the drainage eye rests against the bladder wall, and (3) raise the head of the bed to increase bladder pressure. A shower is safer because sitting in bathwater allows easy bacterial entry into the urinary tract.

saqs.question: List six complications of urinary catheterization and explain how catheter sediment obstruction and painful bladder spasms are managed.
saqs.answer: Six complications: UTI (urethritis, cystitis, pyelonephritis, bacteraemia—most common), paraphimosis, urethral strictures, urethral perforation, bleeding, and altered micturition. Sediment obstruction is often relieved by catheter flushing, while painful bladder spasms causing extrinsic leakage can be alleviated with anticholinergics such as oxybutynin.
